**Wednesday, February 20, 1952**

The Korean War had been frozen for months. American and Chinese forces were dug into positions across the 38th parallel that neither side could break, and armistice talks at Panmunjom had been grinding for more than half a year over a single intractable question: what to do with prisoners of war who refused repatriation. Tens of thousands of men were still dying along a line that hadn't moved in nearly a year. The war had no visible end. You arrived in the middle of it — not at its beginning, not at its end, but in its grinding, inconclusive middle.

---

**Fourteen days earlier**

On February 6th, 1952 — two weeks before your birth — King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham. He was fifty-six. His daughter Elizabeth, twenty-five years old, was in Kenya on a wildlife tour when word reached her. She came home a queen.

There is something worth sitting with in the timing. Britain in February 1952 was not the Britain of 1900, or even 1930. The empire was visibly contracting. India had been independent for five years. The Marshall Plan had made clear where power now resided. A young woman ascending to a throne over a kingdom still emerging from wartime rationing — food rationing in Britain would last two more years — was inheriting something both immense and diminished simultaneously. She would reign for seventy years. You were born fourteen days into that reign, and you outlived her: she died in September 2022, when you were seventy.

---

**Your tenth birthday**

On February 20, 1962, John Glenn sat inside a capsule called Friendship 7 and became the first American to orbit the Earth. He circled the globe three times in less than five hours, then splashed down in the Atlantic. It was your tenth birthday.

The achievement mattered beyond the spectacle. The Soviet Union had beaten the United States into space, into orbit, into nearly every early milestone of the space race. Glenn's flight didn't close that gap, but it stopped the psychological bleeding. The decade of your childhood would end with twelve Americans walking on the Moon. You were seventeen for the first of them.

---

**Ten years before you were born**

On February 20, 1942 — exactly a decade before your birth — a Navy lieutenant named Butch O'Hare flew his Grumman Wildcat alone into nine Japanese bombers bearing down on the aircraft carrier Lexington. He shot down five in roughly four minutes and drove off the rest. He was awarded the Medal of Honor — the Navy's first of the Second World War. When Chicago eventually rebuilt and expanded its main airport, they named it after him. Every flight into O'Hare International still lands at a field carrying his name, though most passengers have no idea why.

You arrived exactly ten years after his four minutes.

---

**Your thirty-fourth birthday**

On February 20, 1986, the Soviet Union launched the core module of Mir into orbit — the space station that would serve as a permanent outpost for fifteen years, host cosmonauts and astronauts from twelve nations, and survive the collapse of the country that built it before being deorbited in 2001. It was your thirty-fourth birthday. The Cold War that had defined your entire childhood and young adulthood was still three years from its visible end, but the machine that would outlast the Soviet Union went into orbit on the day you turned thirty-four.

---

**The world you entered**

In February 1952, television had reached roughly a third of American homes, but the medium was still tentative — still learning what it was. Radio carried the news. Most households had never flown in an airplane. The polio epidemic of 1952, one of the worst in American history, was still months ahead; the Salk vaccine that would end it wouldn't be announced until 1955. The nuclear arms race was accelerating: the United States was preparing to test its first hydrogen bomb in the fall. The Soviet Union had already detonated its first atomic device three years earlier. Fallout shelters were being planned. Children were being taught to crouch under desks.

The world held roughly 2.5 billion people. It holds more than three times that now.

---

**The arc**

You are 74. You were born before commercial jet passenger service, before the interstate highway system, before the polio vaccine, before rock and roll had a name. You were a teenager when Kennedy was assassinated. You watched the moon landing in your late teens. You were in your thirties when the personal computer arrived as a consumer product, your forties when the internet became public, your fifties on September 11, your mid-sixties when smartphones were already ubiquitous, your seventies now as artificial intelligence produces coherent prose on demand.

The queen who was fourteen days into her reign when you were born is gone. The Soviet Union that shadowed every decade of your childhood is gone. Korea remains divided at almost exactly the same line where the war froze in 1952. The Lexington, the ship Butch O'Hare saved on your birthday's anniversary, was sunk as a target vessel in 1969. Mir burned up over the Pacific in 2001.

What has not gone is the span itself — seventy-four years of a world remaking itself faster than any previous seventy-four, in ways that the people around you on February 20, 1952 would have found largely unimaginable.
